newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltin op could cause limited rouble fall-dealers.
newsitem.headline: Yeltin op could cause limited rouble fall-dealers.

text.p: The rouble, usually impervious to political news, is unlikely to be seriously affected by President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation, even if he dies under the surgeon's knife, currency dealers said on Monday.
Such an outcome would cause the rouble to fall, but the central bank would keep any move within limits, they said.
"Nothing dramatic will happen to the rouble even if the result of the operation is the most unfavourable," United Investment Bank chief dealer Alexander Suchkov said.
Rouble/dollar forward rates could react more actively to such news, he said.

A successful operation would mean the same economic team and policies remain in place. That points to a continuing steady decline of the rouble of two or three points a day, and efforts to bring down yields on government securities, dealers said.
"If Yeltsin is all right, it will be good for all the markets," Suchkov said.
"But the 1997 budget will be the main economic factor. Yeltsin, even in good shape, does not decide everything. The question is how the government will handle it."
Doctors have said Yeltsin's bypass operation may take place this week.
Dealers said Yeltsin's team would be able to run the country until it is clear whether he has made a full recovery or not.

If Yeltsin died demand for dollars would rise, but the central bank would be able to limit any fall just as it has controlled the rouble since July 1995 when it introduced a corridor or upper and lower limits for the currency, they said.

The rouble's fluctuations are now limited by a daily 600-point corridor. The central bank also announces its bid/offer dollar/rouble daily rates with a 10-30 point spread. The rouble has never broken through the limits.
It was 5,456 per dollar on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) on Monday.

Net reserves at the end of July were 19.2 trillion roubles, or $4.14 billion at the end-1995 exchange rate of 4,640 roubles per dollar used by the central bank for accounting. Gross reserves at the end of the first quarter were $19.25 billion.
"The central bank will stop feverish demand (for dollars) but it remains to be seen for how long," Neftekhimbank dealer Vladimir Zrazhevsky said.

Yeltsin's death would mean that a new election should be called within three months. An election campaign would create economic uncertainty, given the poor state of government finances, hurting the rouble, dealers said.
"Banks would shift their investments out of government bonds and into dollars. But a big rouble fall is not likely," said Inkombank dealer Dzhamil Asfari said.
Yeltsin was rarely seen in public since late June. He has spent most of this time in a hospital and a country residence outside Moscow.
